title: I Tried to Fool a Scientific Publisher With AI
gist: A journalist tried to sneak two AI-made papers into IEEE Access: one fabricated with free ChatGPT and Gemini, and one produced by the autonomous research system FARS. Both were caught, the first by ghost citations and the second by heavy preprint reliance and figure artifacts, but the piece argues that peer review cannot absorb AI-scale volume.

insights.claim: A free-chatbot forgery built in roughly two dozen prompts was flagged by IEEE Access automated integrity checks for fabricated references: Gemini found 7, STM Integrity Hub 12 and MolecularConnections could not validate 24.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Reference validation is today's effective filter against cheap AI forgeries.
insights.quote: It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.

insights.claim: The FARS-generated paper had real references but was flagged for a huge percentage of preprint citations and for figure artifacts such as a nonsense line label 'lhewl' and random dots in an AI brain graphic, which the integrity-checking tools did not catch.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Human reviewers still catch what tools miss; tool vendors have a gap to fill.

insights.claim: FARS produced a research proposal in 21 minutes, ran the experiment overnight, and wrote a submission-ready paper in 2 hours after one click each, with the only giveaway being a warning line the author deleted.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Automated research end-to-end timelines are now hours, not months.
insights.locator: Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine

insights.claim: Gemini's own post-hoc audit underestimated the fabricated references in the paper it helped generate, with free models stumbling on references where more advanced LLMs are no longer making such mistakes.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Model capability gains will erode current detection tells.

insights.claim: An estimated 57 percent of published academic articles showed detectable LLM influence by 2025, up from 12 percent in 2023, and over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were completely AI-generated in 2025.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Estimates are detection-based; trust erosion is a systemic risk for scholarly publishers.

insights.claim: For every 40 papers with statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025 only one formally disclosed it, so figures likely underestimate AI involvement.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse

insights.claim: Hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are estimated to be produced annually.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Paper-mill volume pressures publisher integrity budgets.

insights.claim: Retraction Watch cofounder Ivan Oransky likens the crisis to a fire where publish-or-perish is kindling, paper mills are gasoline and AI is the accelerant.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Root cause is incentives, not just AI.
insights.quote: publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant

insights.claim: IEEE Access receives about 60,000 submissions per year and accepts about 20 percent (about 12,000) with at least two reviewers each, while reviewer invitations per article have risen 50 percent since 2018.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Reviewer capacity is a bottleneck; peer-review services and automation tools have a growing market.

insights.claim: IEEE's director of publishing ethics warns that a detection tool built today may not be effective against tomorrow's AI-created paper, leaving the volunteer peer reviewer as the last line of defense.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Detection is a cat-and-mouse game; durable solutions need provenance.

insights.claim: FARS, developed by Singapore-based Analemma, created 166 papers in 417 hours and uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, experimentation and writing; the online service was discontinued after Baidu acquired Analemma.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Big-tech consolidation of agentic research tools; check how Baidu repositions it.

insights.claim: Other automated research systems include AutoResearchClaw, AI Scientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, DeepScientist and LabClaw, which links to autonomous labs generating real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: A crowded field is converging on closed-loop AI science.

insights.claim: An AI Scientist paper and Autoscience Institute papers were accepted through double-blind peer review at ICLR in 2025, so AI-generated work can already pass top-venue review.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Legitimacy thresholds are already being crossed.

insights.claim: Analemma's Xiwen Su argues FARS challenges the paper as the unit of knowledge and predicts a living knowledge graph of well-scoped human and machine contributions with humans focusing on whether research matters.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Vendor view of the future of publishing.
insights.quote: FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge

insights.claim: IEEE Access already automates triage such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submissions and reference validity, and uses AI semantic search to match manuscripts to reviewers; its integrity manager opposes banning AI.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Tool vendors in research integrity are the near-term beneficiaries.

insights.claim: Longobardi suggests scientists may need to prove how they discovered results, with institutions building trust markers such as lab equipment integrated with blockchain; the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces uses unique sample IDs with QR codes and the University of Southampton an electronic lab notebook.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
entities: Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces
insights.so_what: Research provenance tooling is an emerging category, still early.

insights.claim: The author concludes that business-as-usual science is not an option, since defining legitimate AI-conducted research may become harder than detecting outright fraud.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Expect policy shifts at publishers and funders.
